title: Apply basic knowledge of statistics and probability to influence the use of data and procedures in order to investigate life related problems

lessons.title: Collecting and organising data
lessons.html:
What is data?

Data is information we collect, usually as numbers or counts. At work we collect data all the time: the number of carcasses condemned each day, the temperature in the cold room every hour, the moisture of each grain load, or the number of injuries per month. Data helps us see what is happening and make better decisions.

Asking a question first

Start with a clear question. For example: 'On which day of the week do we have the most rejected chickens?' Then decide what data you need: the number of rejected birds each day for four weeks.

Ways to collect data

  • Counting with tally marks on a sheet.
  • Measuring with a thermometer, scale or moisture meter.
  • Asking people questions in a short survey.
  • Using records already kept, like logbooks.

Tally tables

A tally uses lines in groups of five. Four straight lines and a fifth line across make a group of five. This makes counting quick.

Fair data

Data must be collected the same way every time. If one person measures the cold room temperature at the door and another at the back, the data will not be fair to compare. Always follow the procedure for where, when and how to measure. Write the data down straight away so you do not forget, and never make up numbers.

lessons.title: Graphs and averages
lessons.html:
Showing data in pictures

A graph makes data easy to understand at a glance.

Bar graph

A bar graph uses bars of different heights. Each bar shows a category, such as a day of the week. The taller the bar, the bigger the number. Use bar graphs to compare things, like rejects per day.

Line graph

A line graph joins dots over time. Use it to see a trend, like cold room temperature through the day. If the line goes up suddenly, something may be wrong, such as a door left open.

Pie chart

A pie chart is a circle divided into slices. It shows parts of a whole, like how the total weight of a carcass is divided into different cuts.

Finding the average

There are three ways to describe the 'middle' of data. Use these weights of five bags of feed: 49 kg, 50 kg, 50 kg, 51 kg, 55 kg.

  • Mean: add all values and divide by how many. 49 + 50 + 50 + 51 + 55 = 255. 255 ÷ 5 = 51 kg.
  • Median: put values in order and find the middle one. The middle value is 50 kg.
  • Mode: the value that appears most often. 50 kg appears twice, so the mode is 50 kg.

Range

The range shows how spread out the data is: biggest minus smallest. 55 − 49 = 6 kg. A big range in bag weights may mean the filling machine needs checking.

Notice how one heavy bag (55 kg) pulled the mean up. The median is less affected by one unusual value.

lessons.title: Chance and making decisions
lessons.html:
What is probability?

Probability is how likely something is to happen. We use words like impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain.

  • Impossible: a cow laying an egg.
  • Unlikely: snow in Durban in summer.
  • Even chance: a coin landing heads.
  • Likely: rain in the Highveld in summer.
  • Certain: the sun rising tomorrow.

Probability as a number

Probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). It can also be a fraction or percentage. If 5 out of every 100 eggs are cracked, the probability that an egg is cracked is 5 out of 100, which is 0.05 or 5%.

Using past data

We can use records to estimate chance. If a farm's records show that the river flooded the low camp in 3 of the last 10 years, we can say there is about a 3 in 10 chance it will flood next year. This helps the farmer decide whether to move animals before the rainy season.

Using data to solve problems

  1. Ask a clear question.
  2. Collect fair data.
  3. Organise it in a table or graph.
  4. Look for patterns: highest, lowest, trends.
  5. Decide what action to take.

Example: a bar graph shows most knife cuts happen in the last hour of a shift. The team decides to add a short break and check that knives are sharp, because tired workers and blunt knives cause accidents.

Be careful with data

Small amounts of data can mislead. One bad day does not prove a pattern. Collect enough data before you decide.

Key points

  • Start with a clear question, then collect fair data.
  • Bar graphs compare; line graphs show trends; pie charts show parts of a whole.
  • Mean, median and mode describe the middle; range shows spread.
  • Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
  • Use enough data before making a decision.
